newsitem.title: UK: Max Taylor to replace Rowland as Lloyd's chairman.
newsitem.headline: Max Taylor to replace Rowland as Lloyd's chairman.

text.p: Max Taylor, executive director of insurance brokerage Willis Corroon, was nominated as the new chairman of Lloyd's insurance market Wednesday, a spokesman for Lloyd's said.

Taylor, 49, was nominated ahead of former investment bank chief Jonathan Agnew, who was considered by many to be the favourite for the position. Taylor's appointment as chairman is subject to his appointment as a member of Lloyd's ruling council.
The market is expected to see the decision as the choice of the traditional insurance man over the new corporate financier of the type that has come into Lloyd's in the last few years.
His background as a Lloyd's broker bears similarity to that of the outgoing chairman, Sir David Rowland.

Taylor joined Willis Faber and Dumas in the North American aviation division in 1970 and has been with the company for the past 27 years. He was appointed to the board of Willis Faber in 1990 and the Willis Corroon Group in 1993.

Taylor has supported the introduction of technology to the business of insurance. He was chairman of the London Insurance Market Network (LIMNET) for two years until 1994 and played a leading role in the development of the electronic placing and processing initiative.

He is on the board of the World Insurance Network (WIN) launched Tuesday and is on a committee set up to oversee the development of electronic commerce in the London market. Also on the board is Lloyd's Chief Executive Ron Sandler.
Earlier this year, Taylor was also elected deputy chairman of the Lloyd's Insurance Brokers Committee.
Taylor will take over from Rowland at the end of the year, but the role of chairman may not hold such a high profile as it has in recent years.

Rowland, former chief executive of broker Sedgwick, was the first full-time paid chairman of Lloyd's. He was appointed in 1992 to implement a disaster recovery plan to save Lloyd's from a string of losses totalling 8.1 billion pounds ($13.4 billion).
Constantly in the spotlight of media attention, Rowland finally put the plan into place last year and Lloyd's has now returned to profitability.
Increased emphasis is now being put on the role of Chief Executive Sandler, who has earned a formidable reputation for himself since taking over on the resignation of predecessor Peter Middleton.
